# A Pilgrimage on Screen: Memory, Power, and the Politics of Piety

In the annals of Pakistani political history, few images captured the shifting currents of religious and geopolitical alignment as vividly as the newsreel footage of Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and half his cabinet performing the rites of Hajj. The camera showed these powerful men—accustomed to the trappings of secular authority and Western-educated sophistication—stripped of their usual finery and clad instead in the simple, unstitched white cloth of Ihram. They were shown kissing the Hajar-e-Aswad, the sacred Black Stone embedded in the corner of the Kaaba, and kneeling in postures of humility that few Pakistanis had ever witnessed their leaders adopt in public. This was more than ceremonial theater; it marked a symbolic pivot in the nation's political imagination, signaling a deference toward the rising Islamic influence emanating from Arabia, whose oil wealth and religious authority were beginning to reshape alliances across the Muslim world.

That same year, my father was appointed Hajj secretary by Bhutto himself—a position that placed our family in an unusual and unforgettable vantage point. We were not merely distant observers of this historic pilgrimage; we had, through my father's role, an intimate connection to the very officials and rituals being documented for national audiences. It was a strange convergence of the personal and the political, one that none of us could have anticipated would culminate in a moment of profound family astonishment.

That moment arrived when our entire family—all seven children, our mother, and our ever-present ayah—crowded into the seats of Melody Cinema to watch the newsreel alongside the rest of the moviegoing public. We had come, like everyone else, to witness this landmark event in Pakistan's religious and political life. What we had not expected was to see our own father appear on screen, dressed identically to the Prime Minister in the humble garb of Ihram, walking among the cabinet ministers as though he too were one of the nation's dignitaries performing this sacred duty. The children gasped and pointed at the screen, our ayah clutched her hands to her chest in disbelief, and for a moment, the entire cinema hall seemed to fade away as we absorbed the surreal sight of our father immortalized in newsreel footage beside the most powerful man in the country.

Yet perhaps the most startling revelation of the film was not my father's appearance, but my mother's reaction to a particular scene captured during the rites at Mina. My mother was, by nature and by habit, a woman of near-obsessive cleanliness—what might today be clinically described as mysophobia. She maintained rigorous standards of hygiene in our household, often to the point of exasperating those around her with her insistence on repeated washing and sanitizing rituals before she would touch or eat anything. And yet, on screen, we watched footage of her sitting directly on the ground during an ablution scene, her posture relaxed and unguarded, participating in the ritual purification alongside other pilgrims without any visible hesitation or discomfort. For those of us who knew her daily habits intimately, this was nothing short of astonishing—a woman who could not tolerate a speck of dust on her dining table was shown embracing the dust and earth of Mina with apparent ease and spiritual surrender. It was as though the sanctity of the pilgrimage had temporarily dissolved her deeply ingrained anxieties, replacing them with a humility that transcended her usual compulsions.

In retrospect, this newsreel and the broader spectacle it captured cannot simply be understood as Bhutto's attempt to nationalize or instrumentalize religious piety for domestic political gain, though such an interpretation might seem tempting given his government's later efforts to align more closely with Islamic identity. Rather, the footage represents something more complex and perhaps more telling: a collective submission of Pakistan's political and social elite to the ascendant religious and economic authority of neighboring Arabia. As oil wealth transformed the Gulf states into centers of both financial power and religious legitimacy within the Muslim world, Pakistan's leadership—represented so visibly by Bhutto and his ministers, and by extension, figures like my own father—found itself drawn into a new orbit of deference. The image of these men, stripped of their Western suits and secular postures, kneeling before the Kaaba, spoke to a broader realignment in which Pakistan's elite began to recognize, and perhaps even court, the growing influence of Arabia as a source of both spiritual authority and geopolitical significance in the years to come.

# The Newsreel

The footage opens grainy and unremarkable, the way so much archival film does—men in formal dress moving through crowds, the kind of scene one might scroll past without a second glance. But look closer: that is Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, flanked by his cabinet ministers, and they are not attending a state dinner or a diplomatic summit. They are performing Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, and something in the quality of their movements—the way they shed their tailored suits for simple white ihram cloth, the way they walk among ordinary pilgrims without visible entourage or ceremony—suggests this was not staged for the cameras.

This distinction matters enormously to how we should read the film. It would be easy, cynical even, to interpret such footage as political theater: a leader courting favor with an increasingly influential Arabia, aligning himself with the religious and economic power then consolidating in the Gulf. But the texture of the film resists that reading. There is no grandstanding here, no obvious performance for domestic or foreign audiences. Instead, we see something closer to genuine submission—powerful men making themselves small before a tradition and a holy site that dwarfed their earthly authority.

I have a particular stake in this footage, one that transforms it from historical curiosity into something achingly personal. My father served as Hajj secretary that year, which meant our family did not simply watch this pilgrimage from afar—we were embedded within it, present for the logistics, the ceremony, the human texture that rarely survives in official records. This is not distant history to me; it is inherited memory, passed down through my father's recollections and, remarkably, preserved on film.

And it is within this personal dimension that the newsreel achieves its most unexpected power. Amid the shots of ministers and dignitaries, the camera captures something I could never have anticipated: my mother, kneeling on the ground, participating in the communal ablution rituals alongside strangers.

To understand why this moment stops me every time I watch it, you would need to know my mother as I knew her—a woman of exacting fastidiousness, someone whose relationship with cleanliness bordered on the clinical, who recoiled from shared utensils and treated communal space with wary suspicion. She was, by any account, someone who guarded her physical boundaries with vigilance. And yet here she was, on camera, lowering herself to the same dust that thousands of other pilgrims had touched, performing ablution in full view of strangers, her carefully maintained boundaries dissolved by something larger than her own discomfort.

This is the moment the newsreel truly earns its subject. Watching my mother submit to that ritual, I understand something about the pilgrimage that no amount of footage of Bhutto and his ministers could convey: that Hajj does not simply ask for outward performance of humility—it demands genuine transformation, however briefly, of the self one carries into it. If a prime minister could set aside the trappings of state power, and if my own mother could set aside her most deeply held personal boundaries, then perhaps this is the truest evidence the film offers: that something in Mecca that year proved larger than any human authority, political or personal, willing to encounter it.

# A Journey of Humility

The concept of humbling experiences transcends cultures and continents, finding powerful expression in both personal history and sacred tradition.

Benazir Bhutto, Pakistan's first female Prime Minister, understood humbling moments intimately. Her political career was marked by dramatic reversals of fortune—rising to lead a nation, only to face exile, imprisonment, and the constant threat of violence. Despite commanding immense political power, she often spoke of moments that reminded her of her own vulnerability and the weight of responsibility she carried for her people. Her assassination in 2007 stood as a stark reminder that even the most powerful figures remain subject to forces beyond their control—perhaps the ultimate humbling experience.

Mecca, the holiest city in Islam, represents humbling on a spiritual and universal scale. Each year, millions of Muslims undertake the Hajj pilgrimage, arriving from every corner of the globe, from every economic background and social status. Within the sacred boundaries of Mecca, distinctions of wealth, nationality, and rank dissolve. Pilgrims wear simple white garments called ihram, symbolizing equality before God. Kings and paupers circle the Kaaba together, all reduced to the same humble posture of devotion. This ritual act of humbling oneself before something greater than personal ambition or identity has drawn believers for over fourteen centuries.

The connection between these two subjects—a stateswoman's turbulent political journey and a sacred city's timeless spiritual practice—reveals a universal truth: humbling experiences, whether thrust upon us by circumstance or deliberately sought through faith, often teach the most profound lessons about our place in the world. Bhutto herself, as a Muslim leader, would have understood the significance of Mecca's teachings on humility, even as she navigated the complex, humbling realities of power in the modern political arena.

Both remind us that true strength often emerges not from domination, but from the recognition of our shared human vulnerability.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary short passage in the style of a Pakistani memoir, describing a family watching a newsreel of their father's Hajj pilgrimage under Bhutto's government, with rich historical and sensory detail.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Screening

The reel arrived three weeks after Abba returned, summoned from the PTV offices in a tin canister that Chacha Rasheed carried against his chest like something holy. We had waited through the autumn of 1976 for this—the year Bhutto's government had begun sending official cameramen with the Hajj delegations, part of some new ministry initiative to document "Pakistan's spiritual diplomacy," though none of us understood then what that phrase would come to mean.

The projector's hum filled our drawing room in Gulberg, the walls still smelling of the fresh whitewash Ammi had insisted upon for the occasion. Neighbors crowded onto borrowed chairs from the Siddiquis next door. Nani sat closest to the sheet we'd hung against the almirah, her tasbih moving without pause, as if the black and white flickers required her continued prayers to hold their shape.

When Abba's face first appeared—grainy, sun-darkened, dwarfed by the white ihram that made him look like every other man and like no man at all—my mother made a sound I had never heard her make before. Not quite a sob. Something older than grief.

The camera showed the Kaaba wreathed in that impossible crowd, thousands moving as one creature, and somewhere in that tessellated humanity was my father, though we could not find him in the wide shots, only trust that he was there. Chacha Rasheed kept pausing the reel to point at strangers—"Is that him? By the pillar?"—until Ammi told him to be quiet, let it play, let it breathe.

The government voice-over, stern and formal, spoke of unity, of the Ummah, of Pakistan's place among nations. But beneath those words we heard other things: the shuffle of a million sandals on stone warmed by God knows how many centuries of sun, the murmur of talbiyah rising like smoke, indistinguishable voices braided into a single supplication that seemed to include, somehow, our small gathering in Lahore, watching a rented projector throw light onto a bedsheet, believing—the way only families recently separated can believe—that somewhere in that ocean of white cloth, we had glimpsed the exact shape of our own waiting.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a paragraph of creative nonfiction about growing up in 1970s Pakistan, focusing on a scene at a cinema where the narrator's family sees themselves on screen during a Hajj documentary, blending political commentary on Bhutto with personal memory.
counterfactuals.output: The projector's beam cut through cigarette smoke and the particular darkness of Karachi's summer power cuts, when the generator would cough to life just for cinemas and government offices, as if entertainment and bureaucracy were the twin pillars holding up the nation. We had gone that year, my father in his good white shalwar kameez, my mother adjusting her dupatta with the nervous energy of someone unaccustomed to being documented, all of us folded into the crowd at Mecca performing the same ancient rites that had drawn pilgrims for fourteen centuries—and now here we were again, flattened onto a screen at Bambino Cinema, our actual bodies made ghostly and public, circling the Kaaba in grainy newsreel footage that PIA had commissioned, ostensibly to celebrate Pakistani participation in Hajj but really, everyone understood, to remind us that Bhutto's government had arranged the flights, subsidized the pilgrimage, wrapped Islamic piety around socialist rhetoric like a flag around a fist. My mother gasped and gripped my wrist when she recognized her own green dupatta in the crowd, and for a moment the theater's four hundred strangers became witnesses to our family's small eternity, our one trip to the House of God recorded not by choice but by the state's hunger for images of its own righteousness. Bhutto himself never appeared in the footage, but his absence was its own kind of presence—the way his portraits hung in every government building we'd had to visit for the visa paperwork, the way his voice on the radio promised roti, kapra, aur makaan while inflation ate through whatever roti we could afford, the way even our devotion, our most private communion with the divine, had been quietly annexed into propaganda for a Prime Minister who would be hanged within two years, his own image eventually erased from those same government walls. I remember only the wonder of seeing myself made larger than life, a child's face flickering twenty feet tall, unaware that I was watching the last summer before everything—the country, the Prime Minister, my own understanding of what was permanent—began to unravel.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a densely allusive, essayistic piece of prose that intertwines Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's political image with a childhood memory of a Hajj newsreel, using vivid, ironic details about class, piety, and family hygiene.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Newsreel

Before I understood what it meant to be Prime Minister, I understood what it meant to be photographed. Bhutto in the black sherwani, Bhutto with the astrakhan cap tilted at an angle that suggested both Oxford and Larkana, Bhutto at the podium in Lahore promising bread and roti and cloth as though he had never eaten with a fork in his life. The image was the argument. The image was, in fact, the only argument that mattered to a nation still learning to read.

I was perhaps seven when the newsreel played before the Sunday matinee — some grainy dispatch from Mecca, pilgrims in white ihram flowing like a spilled bag of flour down the marble concourse, and my grandmother, who had never been and would never go, wept into her dupatta with a devotion so pure it embarrassed the rest of us into silence. My father, who considered himself modern in the way that men who still ate with their hands considered themselves modern, muttered that half those pilgrims in the front rows were ministers and mill-owners who'd flown in on someone else's foreign exchange, performing poverty for the cameras the way Bhutto performed socialism from a two-hundred-acre estate.

This was the genius of the era: everyone was performing something, and everyone knew it, and the knowing didn't stop the performance. The feudal in Sindh who could not read his own land deeds stood before a crowd and spoke of *awam*, of the people, as though he were one broken loaf among many. The newsreel cut from the Kaaba to a shot of dignitaries disembarking, and I remember thinking even then — a child, sticky with the barfi my grandmother pressed into my palm to stop my fidgeting — that piety and power wore the same white cloth, differently laundered.

Because that was the other lesson, the domestic one, the one that never made it into any speech. My grandmother boiled our drinking water twice and would not let the sweeper's child touch our steel tumblers, but she called Bhutto a man of the people and meant it, the contradiction never once catching in her throat. Class in our house was hygiene wearing the mask of hospitality: you fed the poor at the gate, on a separate plate, with a separate god watching. Bhutto understood this arithmetic better than any man of his class had a right to — he who bathed, surely, in water no sweeper's hand had blessed, who nonetheless stood in the jute mills of Punjab promising a new dispensation, his voice cracking at the exact register of sincerity that made men weep the way my grandmother wept at pilgrims she'd never meet.

I think now that the newsreel and the podium were the same reel, spliced by the same censor's hand, both selling us the same fantasy: that proximity to the sacred — Mecca, the masses, the mythology of the common man — could be borrowed like a sherwani, worn for the length of a speech, and returned to the wardrobe before dinner. My grandmother died still believing in both fictions. I inherited her tumblers, and her doubt, several years too late to ask her which one she'd chosen, in the end, to keep her faith in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary vignette in a Salman Rushdie–like voice, mixing historical irony and personal nostalgia, about a Pakistani family's experience watching their father's pilgrimage to Mecca dramatized in a state newsreel under Bhutto's rule.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Small Man Made Large by the Grace of the State**

In the year that Mr. Bhutto discovered God—or rather, discovered that God, properly filmed, could be made to serve the Five-Year Plan as reliably as tractors and fertilizer—my father went to Mecca and returned to find that he had been nationalized.

This was 1974, or perhaps 1975; in our family, as in our country, dates were the first casualties of retelling. What is certain is that Abba went as a private man, a textile merchant with flat feet and a fondness for pistachio kulfi, carrying in his suitcase seventeen small prayer rugs to distribute among relatives who would forever after claim they had never received them, and he came back three weeks later to discover that Pakistan Television had somehow acquired eleven minutes of newsreel footage in which he could clearly be seen—third row, white ihram slipping from his left shoulder in a manner his mother would have found deeply improper—circumambulating the Kaaba while a baritone voice-over informed the nation that under the visionary leadership of Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, Islamic Socialism was carrying the faithful of Pakistan closer to God than ever before in the history of the Ummah, closer, one gathered, than they had traveled under previous godless regimes, as though the Kaaba itself had shuffled a few strategic meters nearer to Larkana.

We watched this footage in our drawing room in Karachi eleven times, my mother counting each viewing on her fingers like tasbih beads, my sister Naila weeping with a confusion she would spend the next decade trying to name, and I—eight years old, congenitally smart-mouthed, already rehearsing the treasons of memory that would later become my profession—I asked the only sensible question in the house: "Abba, did you know they were filming?"

He had not known. This was the genius of the age: the state filmed you performing your most private transaction with the Almighty and then presented the footage back to you as evidence of its own benevolence, so that even your prayers became a kind of testimonial, even your surrender to God got itself endorsed, like a soap powder, by the Ministry of Information. Bhutto—who kept, we were later assured by servants who should have known better, a well-stocked bar in a country he had just declared alcohol-free for everyone except foreigners and, apparently, presidents—Bhutto understood before any of us that piety was the only currency that inflated rather than depreciated, and he spent my father's Hajj like small change, buying legitimacy one devout citizen at a time, the whole nation assembled into a single enormous supplication with himself, somehow, at the qibla.

My father, to his eternal credit, found the entire episode hilarious. "I went to see God," he said, "and I came back and saw myself on television instead. Which of these do you think was the more convincing miracle?" He said this while doing an impression of the newsreel voice-over, the baritone made ridiculous, which was Abba's specialty: reducing history to a joke small enough to fit inside a joke, the only sane response, he believed, to a country that kept confusing the size of its rhetoric with the size of its soul.

Years later, after the hangings and the coups, after Bhutto himself had been swallowed by the very apparatus of theater he'd perfected—martyred, canonized, reduced in his turn to eleven minutes of somebody else's footage—I would think of my father's face on that screen, slightly out of focus, performing devotion he had not known was a performance, and I would understand that this was the peculiar curse and comedy of our nation: that even our holiest journeys could be requisitioned by the state and returned to us starring ourselves, that the government could not build a functioning railway but could, with terrifying competence, nationalize a man's soul between the Departure and Arrival lounges of Karachi airport.

We kept no copy of the footage. Of course we didn't—who did, in those days, keep copies of anything, when the state was so generously keeping copies of us?
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short narrative reflection exploring themes of religious performance, political spectacle, and family identity, centered on a scene of watching Bhutto and one's own father in Ihram at a cinema in Lahore or Karachi.
counterfactuals.output:
# The White Cloth

The newsreel flickered before the feature began—that was how it worked in those days, a ritual of waiting that no one questioned. My father had taken me to the cinema in Lahore, ostensibly for the film, but I suspect now that he already knew what preceded it. He always seemed to know things before they announced themselves.

There was Bhutto, wrapped in the two seamless sheets of Ihram, performing Umrah before the cameras. The unstitched cloth that was supposed to erase all distinction—prince indistinguishable from pauper, minister from mason—somehow, on him, became distinction itself. The way it draped, the way he held his hands, the careful angle toward Mecca chosen as much for God as for the lens. I remember thinking, even as a boy, that I was watching a man wear humility the way other men wear medals.

Beside me, my father shifted in his seat. He had worn the same white cloth himself, years before, without any camera to record his devotion. I had seen the photographs at home—small, curling at the edges, kept in a drawer rather than a newsreel. His Ihram had been just cloth. Bhutto's was costume and confession at once, a garment doing double duty as prayer and as propaganda.

"They are the same cloth," my father said quietly, not looking at me, "but not the same nakedness."

I didn't understand him then. I think I do now. My father's pilgrimage had been a private erasure—an attempt to become, briefly, no one in particular before God. Bhutto's was a public assertion of exactly who he was: a leader humbling himself so that the nation might watch him do it, so that piety might become a kind of political currency, spent in the very moment it was performed.

And yet—was my father entirely innocent of performance? He had, after all, brought me to see this. He wanted me to notice the difference between the two Ihrams, which meant he wanted me to understand something about himself as much as about Bhutto. Even privacy, once it is narrated to a son, becomes a kind of theater.

We watched the screen together, father and son, while a politician's borrowed sanctity flickered above us in grainy black and white. I have thought of that evening many times since—how identity is never simply given but always, in some measure, performed; how even the cloth that is supposed to strip us of distinction can become, in the wrong hands or the right lighting, a stage.

The feature began. I don't remember what we saw. I remember only the white cloth, and my father's silence afterward, and the strange inheritance of watching someone else's devotion while sitting beside the memory of your own father's.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
